subtype: Approach: assume nothing is at risk because nothing was stolen [Pitfall]
passage:
When the news said Omar's fitness app had leaked email addresses, he shrugged. "Only my email. No password, no card. Who cares?" His sister Mina, visiting from Toronto, raised an eyebrow, but Omar had already returned to the video game.

Three months later an email arrived with his full name, his gym's name and a photo taken from his public profile. It said his membership was overdue and asked him to pay a small fee through a link. It looked so personal that he clicked, and only stopped at the payment page when Mina looked over his shoulder and said, "How would they know all that?" The fee was fake, and Omar spent the evening changing passwords and feeling foolish about what small pieces add up to.

qa.q: What did Omar say when he learned about the leak?
qa.a: Omar said it was only his email, with no password or card, and asked who cared.

qa.q: How did Omar feel when Mina stopped him at the payment page?
qa.a: Omar felt foolish and shaken, realising he had nearly been fooled by a message that seemed personal.

qa.q: What could Omar do to protect himself against such messages in future, and why?
qa.a: Omar could check any unexpected fee by going to the gym directly, because a real membership issue can be confirmed without using the link.

qa.q: How does Mina see Omar's first shrug compared with what happened later?
qa.a: Mina had raised an eyebrow because a leaked address may join other details, so the later personal email showed her doubt was fair.

grounding: The person assumes an email-only leak is harmless, but later the address combined with other data enables a targeted scam.
